lead: A sensor turns a physical quantity — temperature, pressure, position, speed — into an electrical signal. That signal is often small, noisy and nonlinear, so signal conditioning amplifies, filters and shifts it before an ADC converts it to a number for the ECU. An error at the sensing element becomes a wrong fuel pulse or brake force. This chapter fixes the vocabulary, classifies sensors, and follows the signal to the ECU input.
prereq: You need Ohm's law, the voltage divider and a stable DC supply from Unit 1; the thermistor returns in 3.5.

sections.h3: Sensor, transducer, actuator, and the words used to judge them

blocks.text: A sensor converts a physical quantity into an electrical signal. The quantity it measures is the measured variable — coolant temperature, manifold pressure, wheel speed. The transducer is the element that does the conversion; most automotive writing uses both words for the same part. An actuator works the other way: an electrical command becomes motion or force, covered in 3.8.
Specifications decide whether a sensor suits a job. Each word below has a precise meaning; marks are lost when units are dropped.

items: Range: the lowest and highest input the sensor is specified for, e.g. −40 °C to 150 °C.
Span: range maximum minus range minimum, e.g. 190 °C.
Sensitivity: output change per unit input change, e.g. 10 mV/°C. It always carries units.
Resolution: the smallest input change that gives a detectable output change.
Accuracy: how close the reading is to the true value, quoted as ±°C or as a percentage of full scale.
Linearity: how far the input–output graph bends away from a straight line, as a percentage of full scale.
Hysteresis: the output gap at the same input when the input arrives from below rather than from above.
Drift: slow change of output with time or ambient temperature while the input is held constant.
Response time: time for the output to reach a stated fraction (often 63% or 90%) of its final value after a step input.

sections.h3: Classification and the sensing elements inside

items: Active vs passive: a passive sensor generates its own signal (thermocouple, piezoelectric element, magnetic reluctance coil); an active sensor needs an excitation supply (thermistor, potentiometer, biased Hall device). Some instrumentation textbooks use the reverse convention — active for a self-generating element such as a thermocouple — so state which convention you are using in an answer.
Analog vs digital: analog sensors give a continuous voltage; digital ones give a pulse train whose frequency or count carries the value.
Contact vs non-contact: a coolant thermistor touches the fluid; a Hall or optical sensor reads a target across an air gap.
Absolute vs relative: an absolute sensor measures from true zero (manifold absolute pressure from vacuum); a relative sensor measures against a local reference such as ambient pressure.

blocks.text: Behind these classes sit a few physical effects. Resistive elements change resistance with position, temperature or strain (potentiometer, NTC thermistor, strain gauge). Capacitive elements change capacitance with diaphragm movement or humidity. Inductive and magnetic-reluctance elements produce a voltage from changing flux. Piezoelectric crystals produce charge under force, used for knock. Thermoelectric junctions (thermocouples) produce a small voltage proportional to temperature difference. Hall elements give a voltage proportional to magnetic field. MEMS devices etch a silicon diaphragm or proof mass so the sensing element and its conditioning circuit sit on one chip.

sections.h3: Signal conditioning: from millivolts to a number

blocks.text: Signal conditioning is everything between the sensing element and the ADC. It makes a weak, noisy, offset, nonlinear signal into a clean voltage in the ADC's input window.

items: Excite and bridge: a Wheatstone bridge turns a small resistance change into a differential voltage that sits near zero when the input is zero.
Amplify: an instrumentation amplifier multiplies the differential voltage by a fixed gain and converts it to a single-ended signal referred to ground.
Filter: a low-pass filter removes ignition and switching noise; its corner is f = 1/(2πRC), with R in ohms and C in farads.
Isolate: optocouplers or capacitive barriers separate high-voltage battery sensors from the low-voltage ECU.
Linearise: a lookup table or polynomial maps the raw reading to engineering units, because thermistors and bridges are not straight lines.
Cold-junction compensation: a thermocouple measures only a difference, so the ECU adds the measured temperature of the connector block.
Sample and hold: a capacitor freezes the voltage while the ADC converts, so a changing input does not smear the result.
ADC: an N-bit converter reports a count, count = round(V × (2^N − 1) / V_ref), where V is the input in volts and V_ref is the reference in volts.

blocks.where: V_out is the junction voltage in volts; V_s is the supply voltage in volts; R_s is the sensing resistance in ohms, connected from V_out to ground; R_f is the fixed resistor in ohms, connected from +V_s to V_out.

examples.question: A coolant temperature sensor uses a 1 kΩ fixed resistor R_f from +5 V to the output node, and an NTC thermistor R_s from the output node to ground. R_s is 2 kΩ at 25 °C and 0.5 kΩ at 80 °C. (a) Find the divider output at both temperatures. (b) Find the 10-bit ADC counts for a 0–5 V ADC. (c) State the ADC resolution in mV.
steps: Divider equation: V_out = V_s × R_s / (R_s + R_f), with V_s = 5 V and R_f = 1000 Ω. R_f connects +5 V to V_out; R_s connects V_out to ground.
Check the direction: resistance falls as temperature rises (NTC), so the output falls too. The count-to-°C map is nonlinear and is done by lookup table in the ECU.
examples.answer: The divider gives 3.333 V (682 counts) at 25 °C and 1.667 V (341 counts) at 80 °C, with 4.89 mV per ADC count.
examples.check:
Vs = 5.0
Rf = 1000.0
for R in (2000.0, 500.0):
    V = Vs * R / (R + Rf)
    print(round(V, 3))
    print(round(1023 * V / Vs))
print(round(5 / 1023 * 1000, 2))

traps: The ADC count is not the physical value. 682 is a voltage code, not 25 °C; convert and linearise with the sensor curve before quoting a temperature.
NTC resistance falls with temperature, so the divider output falls with temperature. Many answers show the voltage rising and lose all the marks.
Sensitivity must carry units (mV/°C, mV/kPa). A bare number is treated as incomplete.
Resolution is not accuracy. A 10-bit ADC resolves 4.89 mV, but the sensor may still be accurate only to ±2 °C; reference tolerance and self-heating add further error.
Self-heating: the excitation current through a thermistor adds heat and shifts the reading, and a drifting 5 V reference scales every count you compute.

quiz.q: Define sensor and transducer. In automotive writing the two words usually name the same part; state what a transducer can additionally mean.
quiz.a: A sensor converts a physical quantity into an electrical signal; the transducer is the element performing the conversion. In automotive practice the words are used interchangeably; a transducer can also mean a device that converts one form of energy into another, for example a pressure capsule that converts pressure into a voltage.

quiz.q: Classify as active or passive: NTC thermistor, thermocouple, piezoelectric knock sensor, biased Hall sensor.
quiz.a: Passive: thermocouple and piezoelectric element (they generate their own signal). Active: NTC thermistor and biased Hall sensor (both need an excitation supply).

quiz.q: Why is a Wheatstone bridge preferred to a single divider with a strain gauge?
quiz.a: The bridge gives a differential output near zero at zero strain, so the amplifier sees only the small change; supply drift and temperature effects cancel because they affect both arms equally. A single divider has a large standing offset that must be amplified along with the signal.

quiz.q: Explain hysteresis and drift, with one automotive example of each.
quiz.a: Hysteresis is the output difference at the same input when approached from below versus from above, e.g. a throttle position potentiometer reading slightly differently on press and release. Drift is a slow output change at constant input due to time or temperature, e.g. a pressure sensor reading creeping as the engine bay heats up.

quiz.q: A 1 kΩ fixed resistor sits from +5 V to the output node, with a 1.5 kΩ sensor from the output node to ground. Find the output voltage and the 10-bit ADC count for a 0–5 V ADC.
An 8-bit ADC has a 5 V reference. What input change corresponds to one count?
quiz.a: One count = V_ref / (2^8 − 1) = 5 / 255 = 0.0196 V, that is 19.6 mV. An input change smaller than this cannot be seen.

quiz.q: A coolant thermistor reading climbs steadily for 20 minutes while the engine is off and the temperature is constant. Give two likely causes and one test for each.
quiz.a: First, self-heating: the excitation current warms the element, so compare readings at normal excitation and at a reduced excitation current; self-heating shows as a lower reading at the higher current. A second check is to compute the dissipation V²/R in the thermistor and compare it with the manufacturer's maximum. Second, reference or supply drift: measure V_ref and the 5 V rail against a known standard. A poor ground at the sensor return adds an offset; check the voltage between sensor ground and battery negative.

quiz.q: Why is a sample-and-hold circuit placed before the ADC?
quiz.a: The ADC needs a steady input while it converts. The sample-and-hold capacitor freezes the voltage at the sampling instant, so a slowly changing or noisy signal does not change during conversion and corrupt the digital result.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production sensors move to digital outputs such as SENT and PSI5, where conditioning, linearisation and self-diagnosis sit inside the sensor and the ECU receives engineering units. MEMS integration puts element, amplifier and ADC on one die, making manifold pressure and acceleration sensing cheap. Sensor fusion combines several imperfect sensors — wheel speed, yaw rate and acceleration for stability control — instead of trusting one. Research is active on solid-state gas sensors that survive exhaust temperatures and self-calibrating sensors that correct drift in service. Search terms: smart sensor, SENT protocol, piezoresistive MEMS pressure sensor, sensor fusion, cold-junction compensation.
